source_records.abstract: Temporal networks have gained significant prominence in the past decade for modelling dynamic interactions within complex systems. A key challenge in this domain is Temporal Link Prediction (TLP), which aims to forecast future connections by analysing historical network structures across a range of applications. While existing surveys have addressed specific aspects of TLP, they typically lack a comprehensive framework that distinguishes between representation and inference methods, the two key ingredients of TLP. This survey bridges this gap by introducing a novel taxonomy that explicitly examines representation and inference in existing methods, providing a novel classification of approaches for TLP. We analyse how different representation techniques capture temporal and structural dynamics, examining their compatibility with various inference methods for link prediction tasks. Our taxonomy not only clarifies the methodological landscape but also reveals promising unexplored combinations of existing techniques. This taxonomy provides a systematic foundation for tackling emerging challenges in TLP, including model explainability and scalable architectures for complex temporal networks.

source_records.abstract: This study presents an extension of the conventional data warehouse query paradigm by introducing Multi-dimensional Graph eXpression (MGX), a multidimensional query framework designed to support Online Analytical Processing (OLAP) over graph-based business intelligence data. MGX extends the traditional Multi-Dimensional eXpression (MDX) syntax used in relational data warehouses by incorporating SQL-style analytical constructs, including GROUP BY, HAVING, and ORDER BY, thereby improving the expressive capability and flexibility of multidimensional analysis over graph warehouses. By bridging relational data warehousing technologies with graph-based analytical environments, the proposed framework addresses key limitations of traditional MDX in supporting graph-oriented analytics. It enables more effective exploration of semantically rich and socially connected knowledge embedded in networked datasets. Overall, MGX provides a practical methodological foundation for advancing graph warehousing and supporting next-generation network-centric business intelligence applications.

source_records.abstract: Drug-Drug Interactions (DDIs) often cause significant adverse events, making early identification crucial, especially with rising polypharmacy. While most methods focus on binary prediction, multiclass DDI prediction is more advantageous as it identifies specific interaction types. However, this is challenging due to class imbalance, with many rare interaction types compared to dominant ones. We propose a multiclass DDI prediction framework comprising three components: Stage 1 involves feature extraction, where the molecular structures of two drugs are modeled as graphs using a graph attention network (GAT) as an encoder, then combined with Drug Repurposing Knowledge Graph (DRKG) embeddings to produce enhanced drug features. Stage 2 involves expert modelling, where the paired drug representations are processed by two Mamba State Space Model (SSM)- based experts: a standard Mamba expert and a class-reweighted Mamba expert, which efficiently capture sequential dependencies and interaction patterns between the drug representations. Stage 3 involves gated fusion, where a confidence-based gating strategy integrates the two experts to generate final predictions. The performance on DrugBank and DDIMDL benchmark datasets achieved macro F1 scores of 90.68% and 83.99%, demonstrating our framework’s effectiveness in multiclass DDI prediction. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/devalab/MambaDDI .

source_records.abstract: Detecting adverse Drug-Drug Interactions (DDIs) is critical for patient safety. Graph-based models have advanced DDI prediction by integrating heterogeneous biomedical knowledge. However, most fail to account for patient heterogeneity. Recent work emphasizes that population factors (e.g. age, gender, weight) strongly influence drug outcomes. We built a Neo4j knowledge graph by integrating Canada Vigilance ADR reports, DrugBank, and other biomedical sources. Nodes represent drugs, targets (genes/proteins), diseases, ADR terms, and patient attributes. Patient demographics (age group, sex, weight category) were one-hot or binary encoded and linked to relevant nodes. Embedding patient demographics into the DDI knowledge graph enables more personalized predictions and supports precision medicine goals. This approach can stratify DDI risk by subpopulation and guide safer, individualized prescribing. Key challenges include integrating real-world patient data at scale, handling missing or noisy attributes, and preserving privacy. Nonetheless, demographic-aware knowledge graphs offer a promising path for personalized drug safety assessment.

source_records.abstract: For deep learning-based object identification systems to be more accurate and efficient, feature selection is essential. High-dimensional feature spaces frequently contain redundant or unnecessary data, which raises the danger of overfitting and increases computational expense. In this work, we compare two widely used nature-inspired metaheuristic algorithms for feature reduction in deep learning pipelines: Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO). In order to find an ideal subset of features that maximizes classification performance while minimizing dimensionality, the suggested method combines a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) for feature extraction, PSO, and GWO. Benchmark image datasets are used for extensive experimentation, and the accuracy, F1-score, computational complexity, and convergence behavior of the findings are assessed. Both PSO and GWO considerably reduce the feature set size without compromising model performance, according to our findings, with PSO exhibiting higher robustness and faster convergence in high-dimensional search spaces. This work proposes a scalable approach for real-world object recognition problems and sheds light on the practical trade-offs of swarm intelligence-based optimizers for feature selection.

source_records.abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become a powerful framework for analyzing structured data in the form of graphs, with applications spanning diverse fields such as social networks, biology, and recommender systems. This survey explores methodology, development, and advances in GNN architecture. We methodically survey the major classes of GNNs, including convolutional GNNs (ConvGNNs), spatial–temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs), recurrent-based GNNs (RecGNNs), and graph autoencoders (GAEs). Every model is discussed in terms of underlying mathematical formulations, design principles, and practical applications. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of GNNs for practitioners, students, and researchers alike, highlighting their versatility and potential for future innovations in graph neural networks. This review is broad, addressing the basic ideas behind GNNs, different architectural designs, training and inference methods, common issues and constraints, the variety of datasets used, and real-world applications across numerous fields. We will furthermore discuss applications of graph neural networks across different fields and exemplify open-source codes, benchmark datasets, and model valuation for graph neural networks. In the end, this survey specifies existing challenges in interpretability, generalization, and scalability and proposes possible future research trends to further promote the performance of GNNs across various graph-based learning missions.

source_records.abstract: Contemporary CI/CD practices typically address vulnerability prevention and intrusion mitigation as disjoint activities, which may result in residual risk even after container images pass pre-deployment checks. Pre-deployment scanners can overlook vulnerabilities obscured by image layering or insufficient metadata, whereas runtime detection mechanisms commonly rely on single-source observations and thus fail to capture multi-step exploit chains. This work presents Janus , a coordinated framework for containerized CI/CD security across the pre- and post-deployment phases. Its key idea is that vulnerabilities should be handled according to when they can be addressed most effectively: Janus uses a policy gate to decide which vulnerabilities must be remediated before release and which residual vulnerabilities are explicitly deferred to runtime monitoring. To support pre-deployment decisions under CI/CD time budgets, Janus performs layer-aware incremental scanning and policy-controlled constrained patching on changed image layers. To protect against residual risk after deployment, it enforces the deferred set using abstract, stateful exploit-chain signatures that correlate system and network events through shallow-to-deep runtime inspection. Our evaluation on 346 container images (including all 146 official and 200 widely used community images) shows that Janus improves vulnerability coverage by 42.4% relative to representative scanners in our setup (e.g., Grype, Trivy, CVE-Bin-Tool) while reducing analysis latency by 79.6%. Moreover, on our tested exploit chains, Janus detects all chains that elude representative single-source IDS baselines. These results demonstrate the benefits of coordinating prevention and mitigation across the container lifecycle.

source_records.abstract: Detecting adverse Drug-Drug Interactions (DDIs) is critical for patient safety. Graph-based models have advanced DDI prediction by integrating heterogeneous biomedical knowledge. However, most fail to account for patient heterogeneity. Recent work emphasizes that population factors (e.g. age, gender, weight) strongly influence drug outcomes. We built a Neo4j knowledge graph by integrating Canada Vigilance ADR reports, DrugBank, and other biomedical sources. Nodes represent drugs, targets (genes/proteins), diseases, ADR terms, and patient attributes. Patient demographics (age group, sex, weight category) were one-hot or binary encoded and linked to relevant nodes. Embedding patient demographics into the DDI knowledge graph enables more personalized predictions and supports precision medicine goals. This approach can stratify DDI risk by subpopulation and guide safer, individualized prescribing. Key challenges include integrating real-world patient data at scale, handling missing or noisy attributes, and preserving privacy. Nonetheless, demographic-aware knowledge graphs offer a promising path for personalized drug safety assessment.

source_records.abstract: For deep learning-based object identification systems to be more accurate and efficient, feature selection is essential. High-dimensional feature spaces frequently contain redundant or unnecessary data, which raises the danger of overfitting and increases computational expense. In this work, we compare two widely used nature-inspired metaheuristic algorithms for feature reduction in deep learning pipelines: Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Grey Wolf Optimizer (GWO). In order to find an ideal subset of features that maximizes classification performance while minimizing dimensionality, the suggested method combines a pre-trained convolutional neural network (CNN) for feature extraction, PSO, and GWO. Benchmark image datasets are used for extensive experimentation, and the accuracy, F1-score, computational complexity, and convergence behavior of the findings are assessed. Both PSO and GWO considerably reduce the feature set size without compromising model performance, according to our findings, with PSO exhibiting higher robustness and faster convergence in high-dimensional search spaces. This work proposes a scalable approach for real-world object recognition problems and sheds light on the practical trade-offs of swarm intelligence-based optimizers for feature selection.

source_records.abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become a powerful framework for analyzing structured data in the form of graphs, with applications spanning diverse fields such as social networks, biology, and recommender systems. This survey explores methodology, development, and advances in GNN architecture. We methodically survey the major classes of GNNs, including convolutional GNNs (ConvGNNs), spatial–temporal graph neural networks (STGNNs), recurrent-based GNNs (RecGNNs), and graph autoencoders (GAEs). Every model is discussed in terms of underlying mathematical formulations, design principles, and practical applications. This survey aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of GNNs for practitioners, students, and researchers alike, highlighting their versatility and potential for future innovations in graph neural networks. This review is broad, addressing the basic ideas behind GNNs, different architectural designs, training and inference methods, common issues and constraints, the variety of datasets used, and real-world applications across numerous fields. We will furthermore discuss applications of graph neural networks across different fields and exemplify open-source codes, benchmark datasets, and model valuation for graph neural networks. In the end, this survey specifies existing challenges in interpretability, generalization, and scalability and proposes possible future research trends to further promote the performance of GNNs across various graph-based learning missions.

source_records.abstract: Contemporary CI/CD practices typically address vulnerability prevention and intrusion mitigation as disjoint activities, which may result in residual risk even after container images pass pre-deployment checks. Pre-deployment scanners can overlook vulnerabilities obscured by image layering or insufficient metadata, whereas runtime detection mechanisms commonly rely on single-source observations and thus fail to capture multi-step exploit chains. This work presents Janus , a coordinated framework for containerized CI/CD security across the pre- and post-deployment phases. Its key idea is that vulnerabilities should be handled according to when they can be addressed most effectively: Janus uses a policy gate to decide which vulnerabilities must be remediated before release and which residual vulnerabilities are explicitly deferred to runtime monitoring. To support pre-deployment decisions under CI/CD time budgets, Janus performs layer-aware incremental scanning and policy-controlled constrained patching on changed image layers. To protect against residual risk after deployment, it enforces the deferred set using abstract, stateful exploit-chain signatures that correlate system and network events through shallow-to-deep runtime inspection. Our evaluation on 346 container images (including all 146 official and 200 widely used community images) shows that Janus improves vulnerability coverage by 42.4% relative to representative scanners in our setup (e.g., Grype, Trivy, CVE-Bin-Tool) while reducing analysis latency by 79.6%. Moreover, on our tested exploit chains, Janus detects all chains that elude representative single-source IDS baselines. These results demonstrate the benefits of coordinating prevention and mitigation across the container lifecycle.
